extracted.intended_audience: writers submitting flash nonfiction to Brevity Magazine
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for submitting flash nonfiction (concise literary nonfiction) to Brevity Magazine: pieces must be 750 words or fewer and demonstrate high compression, immediate orientation, strong sound/rhythm, and the ability to suggest larger meaning within a single moment or image.

rubrics_metrics.name: 750 words or fewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Length cap: submissions must be 750 words or fewer ("the 750-words-or-fewer club").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict upper limit; pieces should be concise and self-contained within this word count. The magazine emphasizes very short, compressed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise literary nonfiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepts concise literary nonfiction (with much of the guidance also applying to flash fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect literary craft — careful sentence-level choices, lyrical/evocative language, and narrative compression rather than straightforward reportage or long-form exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: No AI-generated work
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevit y does not accept AI-generated work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions must be the original work of the author; do not submit material generated by AI tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move in and out of scene quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash pieces must 'move in and out of scene quickly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of limited space, scenes must be entered and exited efficiently; avoid prolonged setups or transitional material that dilutes momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce language, diction and rhythm immediately
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the piece's voice and sentence-level musicality from the first lines; there's no room for gradual stylistic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish place, character, conflict, voice right away
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Establish place, character, conflict, voice right away.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key narrative elements should be apparent early so the reader can orient to the piece within very few words; rely on sharp details and implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Working" test: raises interest without confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: "A piece of flash is considered to be working if it raises questions of further interest, but not confusion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful flash suggests larger concerns and invites curiosity while remaining coherent; it should leave apertures rather than unresolved muddiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression — every word load-bearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Compression: every word must be load-bearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate nonessential words; each phrase should contribute meaning, tone, or image. Economy is a central measure of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate orientation — no slow build
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lengthy exposition or gradual ramps; orient the reader immediately to time/place/voice to make use of the small form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resonance density — high meaning per word
rubrics_metrics.description: Resonance density: achieve high meaning per word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack associative, emotional, or thematic resonance into minimal text; use images and phrasing that echo beyond their literal statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single moment / image / insight — can't sprawl
rubrics_metrics.description: Single moment / image / insight: the piece should focus on one concentrated moment, image, or insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flash should not attempt to cover multiple episodes or a wide chronology; pick a single focal point and deepen it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound / rhythm more crucial than in long form
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound/rhythm is more crucial in flash than in long form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to cadence, line-level rhythm, and sonic patterns; sound carries much of the piece's effect when space is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending must surprise but feel inevitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Endings should surprise while feeling inevitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a payoff that recontextualizes what came before; the twist or resolution must be earned by the piece’s internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion over statement — gestures toward larger meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor suggestion over explicit statement; gesture toward larger meaning rather than explaining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust readers to infer implications; use implication and elliptical detail instead of spelling out themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-endedness — aperture rather than closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer open-endedness: create an aperture rather than full closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave space for readers’ imagination and further thought rather than delivering tidy conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Often cited forms in flash (recognized/formal approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common forms: the list essay; the hermit-crab essay (borrowed form); the braided micro-essay; the single-image meditation; the compressed memoir; the scene-as-whole-story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forms are frequently successful in flash nonfiction and can serve as structural templates, but they are not strict requirements; experimentation within the compressed form is encouraged ("a fabulous petri dish for experimentation").
